lessons.title: Growth Phases and Nutritional Needs
lessons.body: Grow-finish pigs go from about 30 kg to 100 kg. This period is split into two phases: grower (30â60 kg) and finisher (60â100 kg). Each phase needs different feed. In Africa, many farmers use commercial pig feeds, but you can also mix your own using maize, soybean meal, fishmeal, and additives. For growers, feed should contain 16â18% crude protein. For finishers, reduce to 14â16% to avoid excess fat and save money. A typical grower diet: 60% maize, 25% soybean meal, 10% fishmeal, 3% wheat bran, 2% minerals and vitamins. Finisher diet: 70% maize, 20% soybean meal, 5% fishmeal, 3% wheat bran, 2% minerals. Always provide clean waterâpigs drink 2â3 times their feed weight. Feed twice daily, at 7am and 4pm. Give each grower 1.5â2 kg per day, and each finisher 2.5â3 kg per day. Adjust based on body condition. If pigs are too thin, increase feed; if too fat, reduce. Never feed moldy maizeâit causes aflatoxin poisoning. Store feed in dry, raised sacks. You can also supplement with kitchen waste or garden vegetables, but cook them first to kill germs. For faster growth, add lysine and methionine (amino acids) at 0.1â0.2% of the diet. These are available at agrovet shops. Weigh your pigs every two weeks to track progress. A well-fed pig should gain 600â800 grams per day. If gain is below 500 grams, check feed quality and health. Remember, feed is 70% of your cost, so buy ingredients in bulk when prices are low. Use a simple feed mixer or mix on a clean tarpaulin. Always keep records of feed used per pig. This helps you know your cost per kg of meat. With good nutrition, you can finish pigs in 5â6 months instead of 8â10 months.

lessons.title: Monitoring Growth and Feed Conversion
lessons.body: To make money from pigs, you must know how well they grow and how efficiently they convert feed to meat. This is called feed conversion ratio (FCR). FCR = total feed eaten divided by total weight gained. For example, if a pig eats 200 kg of feed and gains 80 kg, FCR = 200/80 = 2.5. Good grow-finish pigs have FCR between 2.5 and 3.0. If FCR is above 3.5, you are losing money. Weigh your pigs every two weeks using a pig weighing scale or a weighing tape. A weighing tape is cheap and measures heart girth to estimate weight. For accuracy, use a digital scale if you can afford one. Record weights in a notebook or phone app. Also record feed given each day. At the end of two weeks, calculate average daily gain (ADG). ADG = weight gained / number of days. Target ADG is 700â800 grams per day. If ADG is low, check for worms, disease, or poor feed quality. Deworm every 3 months with ivermectin or albendazole. Also check feed wastageârats, birds, and spillage waste feed. Use feeders that prevent spillage. Monitor water intake: if pigs suddenly drink less, they may be sick. Keep a close eye on the smallest pig in the group; it may be bullied and need separate feeding. Use a simple chart on the wall to track each pen's performance. Compare pens and learn what works. If FCR is poor, try changing feed brand or mixing your own. But always change feed gradually over 5 days to avoid digestive upset. Good monitoring helps you sell at the right time and avoid losses. It also helps you select the best pigs for breeding. Remember, what gets measured gets managed. So measure, record, and act.

lessons.title: Handling and Movement of Growing Pigs
lessons.body: Growing pigs can weigh 30â100 kg. They are strong and can hurt you or themselves if handled roughly. Always move pigs calmly. Pigs have poor eyesight but good hearing and smell. They will follow a bucket of feed. Use a plastic sorting board or a piece of plywood to guide them. Never lift a pig by the ears, tail, or legs. To lift a small pig, hold it under the belly with one arm and support the chest with the other. For larger pigs, use a pig snare or a noose around the upper jaw. But only use a snare for short distances. When moving pigs, work in pairs. One person stands behind, the other guides from the front. Move them slowlyâpigs panic if rushed. Use a race or chute made of metal or wood panels. The chute should be 60â70 cm wide so pigs cannot turn around. If a pig stops, don't hit it. Instead, use a rattle (a plastic bottle with stones) to make noise behind it. Pigs will move away from the noise. For loading onto a truck, build a ramp with a gentle slope (no more than 20 degrees). Put bedding on the ramp to prevent slipping. Never overload a truckâgive each pig 0.5 square meters of space. In hot weather, move pigs early morning or late evening. Provide water before and after transport. If a pig falls, let it rest, then encourage it to stand. Check for injuries. Isolate any injured pig. Always wash your hands and boots after handling pigs to prevent disease spread. Keep a first aid kit with iodine, bandages, and a thermometer. Handle pigs gentlyâthey remember bad experiences and become difficult to move. Good handling reduces stress, which means better growth and fewer health problems.

lessons.title: Environmental Control in Grow-Finish Barns
lessons.body: Grow-finish pigs need a comfortable environment to grow fast. The ideal temperature is 18â22Â°C. In hot African climates, pigs can suffer heat stress. Signs include panting, lying spread out, and reduced eating. To cool pigs, provide shade, open walls for ventilation, and use fans if possible. You can also wet the floor or use sprinklers. But don't make it muddyâmud can cause skin problems. In cold areas, use curtains or plastic sheets to block drafts. Pigs need 0.8â1.0 square meters of space each. Overcrowding causes fighting, tail biting, and poor growth. For a pen of 10 finishers, you need at least 8â10 square meters. Flooring should be concrete for easy cleaning, but provide a dry bedding area with straw or wood shavings. Good ventilation removes ammonia and moisture. Ammonia smell means poor air qualityâopen more vents. Humidity should be 50â70%. If too humid, use fans and remove wet bedding. Lighting: pigs need 8â10 hours of light to eat well. Use natural light or low-energy bulbs. Keep noise lowâloud noises stress pigs. Clean pens daily: remove wet bedding and manure. Disinfect weekly with a safe disinfectant like Virkon. Keep feed and water away from manure. Check waterers dailyâa pig needs 6â10 liters of water per day. In hot weather, they may drink double. Use nipple drinkers or bowls that don't spill. Ensure the water is clean and cool. If you see pigs shivering, add bedding. If they are panting, increase airflow. Monitor temperature with a simple thermometer. Record daily high and low. Adjust curtains and vents accordingly. A comfortable pig eats more and grows faster. This is one of the cheapest ways to improve your profit.

lessons.title: Common Health Issues in Grow-Finish
lessons.body: Grow-finish pigs face several health problems. The most common are worms, respiratory diseases, diarrhea, and skin conditions. Worms cause poor growth and pot-belly. Deworm every 3 months with ivermectin injection or albendazole in feed. Respiratory diseases like pneumonia cause coughing, sneezing, and labored breathing. They are spread by poor ventilation and overcrowding. Treat with antibiotics like oxytetracycline or tylosin, but only under veterinary advice. Diarrhea in growers can be caused by E. coli, salmonella, or coccidia. Signs: watery feces, dehydration, and dullness. Isolate sick pigs and give electrolytes. Use antibiotics if bacterial. For coccidia, use amprolium in water. Skin conditions: mange (mites) causes itching and crusty skin. Treat with ivermectin injection or spray. Ringworm causes round, hairless patchesâuse antifungal cream. Abscesses from fighting need drainage and iodine. Tail biting is a vice caused by boredom, overcrowding, or lack of salt. Provide toys like chains or tires, and add salt to feed (0.5%). If a pig is bleeding, isolate it. Always check hooves for cracks or injuriesâtrim if needed. Vaccinate against swine fever (if in your area) and erysipelas. Keep a health record for each pen: date, symptoms, treatment, and outcome. Quarantine new pigs for 3 weeks before mixing. Use footbaths at barn entrances. Control flies and ratsâthey spread disease. If a pig dies, bury it deep or burn it. Never sell sick pigs for meat. Call a vet earlyâwaiting costs money. A healthy pig grows faster and needs less feed. So prevention is cheaper than treatment. Practice good hygiene, provide balanced feed, and reduce stress. That is your best health plan.

lessons.title: Preparing Pigs for Market
lessons.body: When your pigs reach 90â100 kg, they are ready for market. But preparation starts weeks before. First, check market requirements. Some buyers want 100 kg, others 110 kg. Weigh your pigs and sort by size. Stop feeding antibiotics at least 7 days before slaughterâthis is withdrawal period. Also stop any medicated feed. Continue clean water. Reduce feed slightly 12 hours before transport to reduce vomiting, but do not starve them. Wash pigs with clean water and mild soap to remove dirt and manure. This improves presentation. Check for injuries, abscesses, or herniasâthese reduce price. If a pig is sick, do not sell it. For transport, use a clean truck with bedding. Load during cool hours. Give each pig 0.5 square meters. Do not tie legs. Transport to the market or abattoir as quickly as possible. If selling live, bring a weighing scale and a clean pen. Buyers pay more for uniform, healthy pigs. Group pigs by weight and body condition. Set a fair price based on current market ratesâcheck with other farmers or local radio. Do not accept the first offer if it is too low. Negotiate. If you sell to a butcher, agree on price per kg live weight or carcass weight. For carcass, the dressing percentage is 70â75%. So a 100 kg live pig gives 70â75 kg carcass. Know this to calculate value. After sale, clean and disinfect the truck and pen. Restock only after 1 week. Keep records of sales: weight, price, buyer. This helps you plan next batch. Also, consider selling directly to consumers or restaurants for higher profit. But that requires slaughter facilities and health permits. Start small and build trust. Good preparation gets you better prices and repeat buyers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Grow-Finish Management for African Pig Enterprises

In African pig production, the grow-finish phase (roughly 30 kg to 90â110 kg live weight) is where feed costs, mortality and market timing decide whether a batch makes money or loses it. Feed alone represents 65â75% of total production cost in most small and medium commercial units, so every decision in this phase must be judged against one question: does it increase kilograms of pork sold per kilogram of feed and per day of housing? This reference lesson consolidates the practical benchmarks, tables and checklists you need to run grow-finish pens profitably, with data drawn from FAO, CGIAR/ILRI and other official sources relevant to African conditions.

1. Growth Phases and Nutritional Needs

Grow-finish pigs pass through three practical sub-phases: grower (30â60 kg), finisher (60â90 kg) and heavy finisher/market (90â110 kg). Each has different protein and energy requirements. In Africa, feed is often mixed on-farm using maize, soybean meal, sunflower cake, fishmeal, cottonseed cake, cassava and local by-products. The key is to match crude protein (CP) and lysine to the pig's growth curve, not to feed one ration throughout.

Table 1. Indicative nutrient requirements and feed intake for grow-finish pigs (as-fed basis)
PhaseLive weight (kg)Crude protein (%)Lysine (%)Feed intake (kg/day)Expected ADG (g/day)
Grower30â6016â180.85â0.951.5â2.0600â750
Finisher60â9014â160.70â0.802.2â2.8750â900
Heavy finisher90â11013â140.60â0.702.8â3.2800â950

Source: FAO Animal Production and Health Guidelines; NRC (2012) Nutrient Requirements of Swine, adapted to tropical smallholder ingredients. Values are indicative; confirm with local feed analysis.

2. Monitoring Growth and Feed Conversion

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Weigh a sample of at least 10% of pigs every two weeks, or weigh all pigs at entry, mid-point and exit. Calculate:

  • Average Daily Gain (ADG) = (final weight â initial weight) Ã· number of days
  • Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) = total feed consumed Ã· total weight gained
  • Feed cost per kg gain = FCR Ã cost per kg of feed

Target FCR in well-managed tropical grow-finish units is 2.8â3.2. FCR above 3.5 signals feed waste, poor health, heat stress or unbalanced rations. In African markets where maize and soybean prices swing sharply, tracking feed cost per kg gain weekly is the single most important business indicator.

Table 2. Benchmark performance indicators for grow-finish pigs in African smallholder and medium commercial units
IndicatorGoodAcceptableAction needed
Average Daily Gain (g/day)> 800650â800< 650
Feed Conversion Ratio< 3.03.0â3.4> 3.4
Mortality (%)< 22â4> 4
Days from 30â90 kg< 9090â110> 110
Feed cost per kg gain (USD)< 1.001.00â1.30> 1.30

Source: ILRI/FAO smallholder pig benchmarking, East and Southern Africa; values adjusted to 2024 feed prices.

3. Handling and Movement of Growing Pigs

Pigs are intelligent, social and easily stressed. Rough handling causes bruising, dark firm dry (DFD) meat, reduced growth and increased disease susceptibility. Move pigs in small groups of 5â10, use boards or panels rather than sticks, and never lift pigs by the ears, tail or legs. Work during the coolest hours (early morning or evening) to reduce heat stress. Provide non-slip flooring in alleys and loading ramps. In African markets where pigs are often transported long distances on poor roads, plan rest stops, ventilation and water access â transport stress alone can cost 2â5 kg of carcass weight per pig.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Zoonotic and Handling Risk

Pigs can carry Salmonella, Brucella suis, Erysipelothrix and African Swine Fever (ASF). ASF has no vaccine and no cure â it kills entire herds. Never bring live pigs, pork products or uncooked swill onto your farm without quarantine and veterinary clearance. Always wear boots and gloves when handling sick pigs, disinfect boots between pens, and report sudden deaths to the nearest veterinary officer immediately. Do not sell or move pigs showing fever, skin reddening or abortion.

4. Environmental Control in Grow-Finish Barns

Pigs cannot sweat efficiently. The thermoneutral zone for a 60â90 kg pig is roughly 18â22Â°C. Above 28Â°C, feed intake drops, ADG falls and FCR worsens. In hot African climates, use open-sided barns with ridge ventilation, shade trees, roof insulation (thatch or reflective sheets), wallows or misters, and increased airflow. Ammonia above 20 ppm and hydrogen sulphide above 5 ppm damage lungs and reduce growth. Keep bedding dry, remove wet manure daily, and ensure at least 0.8â1.0 mÂ² per finisher pig. Stocking density above 1.2 pigs/mÂ² increases tail biting, respiratory disease and mortality.

5. Common Health Issues in Grow-Finish

Watch for: respiratory disease (coughing, laboured breathing â often Mycoplasma or Pasteurella), diarrhoea (E. coli, salmonella, worms), mange and lice, erysipelas (diamond-shaped skin lesions), greasy pig disease, and lameness from foot lesions or Mycoplasma hyosynoviae. Deworm every 8â12 weeks using albendazole or ivermectin. Vaccinate against erysipelas and, where available, Mycoplasma. Isolate new pigs for 21â30 days. Keep a simple treatment log with date, pig ID, drug, dose and withdrawal period â this protects both pig health and pork safety for market.

6. Preparing Pigs for Market

Market readiness is a business decision, not just a weight target. Pigs typically reach optimal carcass value at 90â110 kg live weight with 12â16 mm backfat. Beyond 110 kg, FCR worsens sharply and feed cost per kg gain rises. Withdraw feed 8â12 hours before slaughter (water always available) to reduce gut fill and contamination risk. Avoid mixing unfamiliar pigs in the final week â fighting causes bruising and DFD meat. Schedule transport for cool hours, load at 0.5â0.6 mÂ² per pig, and deliver directly to the abattoir or market to reduce shrinkage. In many African markets, selling at 95â105 kg to a known butcher or cooperative gives the best margin and repeat business.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh a sample of pigs every 14 days and record ADG, FCR and feed cost per kg gain.
  2. Match feed CP and lysine to grower, finisher and heavy finisher phases â never one ration throughout.
  3. Keep stocking density at 0.8â1.0 mÂ² per finisher pig and remove wet bedding daily.
  4. Maintain barn temperature below 28Â°C using shade, ventilation and misters in hot months.
  5. Deworm every 8â12 weeks and follow a written vaccination schedule.
  6. Handle pigs calmly in small groups; never lift by ears, tail or legs.
  7. Quarantine all new pigs for 21â30 days and report sudden deaths to a vet immediately.
  8. Withdraw feed 8â12 hours before slaughter; transport in cool hours to reduce shrinkage.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Animal Production and Health â pig sector guidance and good practices
  • ILRI Smallholder Pig Production â East and Southern Africa research and tools
  • WOAH (OIE) African Swine Fever â official disease information and biosecurity
  • National Research Council â Nutrient Requirements of Swine (reference tables)
  • FAO â Pig production and feeding in tropical environments (free PDF)

Business bottom line: In grow-finish, profit is won or lost on three numbers â ADG, FCR and feed cost per kg gain. Measure them weekly, act on them immediately, and your African pig enterprise will convert feed into cash, not just into pigs.

quiz.q: What is the ideal crude protein range for grower pigs (30â60 kg)?
quiz.explanation: Grower pigs need 16â18% crude protein for muscle growth.

quiz.q: How much feed should a finisher pig (60â100 kg) receive per day?
quiz.explanation: Finishers need 2.5â3.0 kg per day to reach market weight efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the target average daily gain for a well-fed grow-finish pig?
quiz.explanation: A healthy pig should gain 600â800 grams per day.

quiz.q: Which amino acids are often added to pig feed to improve growth?
quiz.explanation: Lysine and methionine are limiting amino acids that boost growth.

quiz.q: What is the feed conversion ratio (FCR)?
options: A) Total feed eaten divided by total weight gained
B) Total weight gained divided by total feed eaten
C) Total feed eaten multiplied by weight gained
D) Total water drunk divided by feed eaten
quiz.explanation: FCR = feed intake / weight gain, showing feed efficiency.

quiz.q: What FCR range indicates good performance in grow-finish pigs?
quiz.explanation: An FCR of 2.5â3.0 is efficient; higher means waste.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh grow-finish pigs to monitor growth?
quiz.explanation: Weighing every two weeks allows timely adjustments.

quiz.q: What tool can a small-scale farmer use to estimate pig weight cheaply?
quiz.explanation: A weighing tape measures heart girth to estimate weight.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pig's average daily gain is below 500 grams?
options: B) Check for worms and disease
quiz.explanation: Low gain often indicates health or feed quality issues.

quiz.q: How often should grow-finish pigs be dewormed?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months controls internal parasites.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to lift a small pig?
options: D) Under the belly with support
quiz.explanation: Support the belly and chest to avoid injury.

quiz.q: What should you use to guide pigs without causing stress?
quiz.explanation: A sorting board blocks their vision and guides them calmly.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended slope for a loading ramp?
quiz.explanation: A slope over 20 degrees is difficult and stressful for pigs.

quiz.q: How much space does each pig need on a truck during transport?
quiz.explanation: 0.5 square meters per pig prevents overcrowding and injury.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pig falls during movement?
options: B) Let it rest then encourage it
quiz.explanation: Forcing a fallen pig can cause injury; allow rest first.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for grow-finish pigs?
quiz.explanation: Pigs grow best at 18â22Â°C; outside this they suffer stress.

quiz.q: How much floor space does each grow-finish pig need?
quiz.explanation: 0.8â1.0 square meters per pig reduces fighting and stress.

quiz.q: What does a strong ammonia smell in the barn indicate?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia buildup means poor ventilation and needs immediate action.

quiz.q: How many hours of light per day do pigs need to eat well?
quiz.explanation: 8â10 hours of light supports normal feeding behavior.

quiz.q: How much water does a grow-finish pig drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Pigs need 6â10 liters daily, more in hot weather.

quiz.q: Which disease causes coughing and labored breathing in grow-finish pigs?
quiz.explanation: Pneumonia affects the lungs, causing respiratory signs.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of diarrhea in grow-finish pigs?
quiz.explanation: E. coli and other bacteria cause diarrhea, especially in dirty pens.

quiz.q: How do you treat mange in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin kills mites that cause mange.

quiz.q: What is a common vice in grow-finish pigs due to boredom?
quiz.explanation: Tail biting is a behavioral problem from boredom or crowding.

quiz.q: How long should new pigs be quarantined before mixing?
quiz.explanation: A 3-week quarantine prevents disease spread to the herd.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for antibiotics before slaughter?
quiz.explanation: Most antibiotics require a 7-day withdrawal to ensure meat safety.

quiz.q: What is the dressing percentage for a pig?
quiz.explanation: A 100 kg live pig yields about 70â75 kg carcass.

quiz.q: Why should you wash pigs before market?
quiz.explanation: Clean pigs look healthier and attract better prices.

quiz.q: What should you do with a sick pig before market?
options: B) Treat it and sell later
quiz.explanation: Selling sick pigs is unethical and can spread disease.

quiz.q: How can you get a better price for your pigs?
quiz.explanation: Uniform groups are more attractive to buyers and fetch higher prices.
